e.t: Adida is a proper name, also identified with the form Athitha. It functions as a name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees. The available references preserve the rendering Adida, while the lexical identification also records Athitha. The name appears in 1 Maccabees 12:38 and 13:13, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific person or place being named.

This word means “cat,” referring to the familiar domestic animal. It is a noun, so it names the animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:21. The word’s basic meaning is clear, while the particular significance of that occurrence must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a “darter” or “javelin-man”—someone whose role is to throw a javelin in battle. It identifies a person by military function rather than describing an emotion, action, or general weapon. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, at 1 Samuel 31:3. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its precise role in that passage, but the word itself points to a soldier skilled in using or throwing a javelin.

This adverb means “accurately,” describing an action done correctly, precisely, or in agreement with the facts. It tells the reader how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Deuteronomy and once in Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains careful correctness and precision.

This verb means to “seek again”: to look for someone or something once more. It describes renewed searching rather than a first attempt to find something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Job and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sought and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains a repeated or renewed search. [p03:word:lxx:L700943:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L700943:occurrences]

This noun means “manliness” or “manhood.” It refers to the quality associated with being manly, especially the strength or courage understood by that description. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs nine times, so its central meaning is consistent even though its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. The word is found across Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and later writings, showing that it can describe a recognized human quality rather than a personal name or action.

This word is a proper name: “Ankadēs; Ankathis.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:62. Because the available lexical information gives only the name and not a fuller description, its precise identity must be understood from the surrounding passage rather than from the word alone.

This noun means “relief”: help or support that eases distress, pressure, or need. It names the assistance a person receives when facing difficulty rather than describing the difficulty itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, including passages in Psalms, 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, and Sirach. Its precise shade depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the receiving or provision of needed relief.

This noun means “wandering; error,” describing a departure from the right path or a mistaken course. It can refer either to roaming away or to being wrong in one’s direction or judgment. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is movement or direction that has gone astray.

This verb means to “avert evil by sacrifice.” It describes an action intended to turn away or prevent evil through a sacrificial act. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 16:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on seeking protection from evil by means of sacrifice. It is an action word, focusing on what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or condition.

This adjective describes someone or something that remains steady and does not falter. It conveys dependable firmness rather than hesitation, failure, or wavering. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees, so its central sense is clear even though the individual passages are not provided. The word functions as a description, marking a person or thing as consistently reliable and steadfast. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective means “childless,” describing a person or household without children. It refers specifically to the absence of offspring, rather than serving as a general word for loneliness, barrenness, or lack of descendants unless the surrounding passage gives that sense. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs six times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the same: having no children.

Aphairema, also written Aferema, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings. The name occurs 40 times in the LXX corpus, especially in Numbers, Exodus, and Leviticus. Its precise referent in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

Achlia, also written Akhlia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or named individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:41. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide a broader definition or explain the individual’s role. Its significance in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

Balga, also rendered Valga, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 12:18. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies someone or something named in that passage. Without the verse text and its surrounding context, the precise referent cannot be stated more narrowly. Its meaning is therefore best expressed as the name “Balga” or “Valga,” rather than as a translated concept.

gl: that in which a thing is dipped; dye
d: that in which a thing is dipped; dye

e.t: This noun refers to dye—the substance or liquid in which something is dipped. It names the material used to color an object by immersing it, rather than the object being colored or the act of dipping itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within Judges 5:30. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is the dye or coloring substance associated with dipping.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person or family group called “Banoui” or “Vanoi.” It is not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily the name it identifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times: four times in Ezra and twice in Nehemiah. The references place the name within the post-exilic records of Israel, but the name itself carries no additional meaning stated here.

Geththaios, also rendered Yeththeos, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 12 times in 12 verses, from Joshua through 1 Chronicles. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, its particular reference must be determined from each passage. The name occurs especially in 2 Samuel, where it appears seven times.

This noun refers to an aged person—someone advanced in years. It focuses on age rather than presenting a title, office, or particular character trait. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 20 times, with most occurrences in deuterocanonical books and the remainder in Job and Proverbs. The word appears in passages that refer generally to older people, but the exact significance in any one verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context. Its basic meaning remains a person who is old or aged.

The word means “bodily exercises”: physical training or athletic activity intended to strengthen and discipline the body. It is a noun naming the activity itself, rather than a person who trains or the place where training occurs. In this Greek LXX corpus, it appears four times, all in the deuterocanonical books of 1–4 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Deblatha, also rendered Thevlatha, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. The available lexical meaning identifies it as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. It occurs ten times across ten verses in the LXX, especially in 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough information here to identify the person or place named. Its exact reference is therefore determined by the passage in which it appears.

This noun means “division”: the separating or arranging of people or things into distinct groups, sections, or portions. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially in lists and arrangements connected with Israel’s tribes, priests, Levites, leaders, and their duties. It occurs 32 times across 28 verses, with many occurrences in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding passage determines what is being divided or assigned in each instance.

This Greek LXX noun refers to “equipment” or “furniture”—the movable items prepared for use in a place or activity. It can describe physical furnishings or necessary gear, depending on the surrounding passage. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, including Exodus 31:7 and 2 Maccabees 11:10. Its precise application in either verse depends on the verse’s immediate context, but its central idea remains the set of things arranged or provided for practical use.

This Greek LXX verb means “thoroughly save” or “bring safely through.” It describes delivering someone or something fully out of danger, trouble, or threatening circumstances, with emphasis on reaching safety rather than merely attempting rescue. The word occurs 69 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it can describe repeated acts of safe deliverance across different situations. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject.

This noun means “deceit” or “subtlety”: misleading behavior that hides the truth or uses crafty means to mislead someone. It describes dishonesty as a quality or practice rather than a single spoken falsehood. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Numbers, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains cunning deception.

This Greek LXX noun means “lifting up” or “pride.” It refers to being raised up, or to an elevated attitude that exalts itself. Its basic idea can describe elevation in a straightforward sense or an inward posture of self-importance, depending on the sentence. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 19:25. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which aspect is intended there.

This verb means “burn”: it describes setting something alight or causing it to be consumed by fire. It presents burning as an action rather than naming the fire or the object involved. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 2:29. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being burned and how the action functions in that passage.

This noun refers to a nation or a distinct social group, described here as a caste. It can identify a people considered together as a community rather than one individual. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented by this LXX corpus, it appears 916 times, showing broad use for peoples and collective groups. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and whether the context emphasizes a nation, a people group, or a social class.

This Greek LXX noun means “twentieth,” referring to the twentieth item, day, month, or other numbered position in a sequence. It is an ordinal number rather than a general quantity: it identifies something that comes after the nineteenth and before the twenty-first. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Ezra, Esther, Haggai, and the Maccabean books. Its precise significance in any verse depends on the calendar, reign, date, or sequence being described there.

This word means “hundred,” the number equal to ten groups of ten. It functions as a number, identifying how many people, objects, or units are being counted. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 208 times, showing regular use in biblical statements involving quantities. Its ordinary meaning remains numerical; the surrounding words determine what is being counted and whether the number is exact or part of a larger amount.

This Greek verb means “emerge” or “travel out.” It describes going outward from a place, source, or point of origin, and functions as an action word in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 158 times, showing regular use for movement outward across many kinds of passages. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing is moving and where it is going.

This Greek LXX verb means “cry out”: to call aloud or express words in a strong, audible outcry. It describes an action of speaking publicly or forcefully, rather than simply mentioning something quietly. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all within Daniel 2, so its established sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in each occurrence depends on the immediate sentence and passage context.

This noun refers to a silver fir, a kind of fir tree. It names a physical tree rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs eight times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Psalms, Ezekiel, and other books. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the silver fir itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “see in”: it describes seeing or looking within something. As a verb, it expresses an act of perception rather than naming a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, at Genesis 20:10. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains an act of seeing inward or within.

Ennon is a proper name, rendered “Ennōn” or “Ennon.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 42:17. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not establish whether Ennon refers to a person, place, or another named entity, so its precise referent must be determined from the verse and its surrounding context.

This verb means “sharpen”: to make something keen or pointed, especially an edge or weapon. It describes an action rather than a person, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 21:16. The central idea is purposeful preparation by making something sharper and more effective. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, whose text is not included here.

ἑορτή is a noun meaning “festival” or “feast”—a recognized occasion for communal celebration. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, it regularly refers to a named or customary celebration rather than an ordinary meal. The word occurs 111 times in this corpus, indicating broad and repeated use. Its precise significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains a festival or feast.

This word means “battlement,” a raised wall or protective structure built along the edge of a city wall, tower, or building. It describes a physical defense that helps protect those inside and gives defenders a position above or along the wall. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including passages from 1 Kings, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Adjudicate” means to make a formal judgment or decision, especially when a matter must be settled. It is a verb describing the act of deciding an issue rather than the person or authority who decides it. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, in two different verses. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here; the word itself points to judgment that settles a matter.

This verb means to thoroughly testify—to give firm, serious testimony about something. It describes more than merely mentioning a matter; it expresses bearing witness clearly and fully. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it appears seven times, including several passages where people testify or bear witness. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a deliberate, thorough declaration of what is known or affirmed.

This word is a proper name, referring to “Euzai,” also given as “Efze.” It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea; it identifies a named person or designation in the Greek LXX wording. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Nehemiah 3:25. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be stated from the word alone.

This noun means “straightness” or “direction.” It describes what is straight, rightly directed, or set on a clear course. In the Greek Old Testament, the word can express the quality of a straight path or the proper direction of conduct, depending on the surrounding sentence. It occurs 22 times in the LXX corpus, mostly in Psalms, and is also found in historical and wisdom books. Its central idea remains directness rather than crookedness or confusion.

This Greek LXX noun refers to age or adulthood—the stage or measure of a person’s life. It can describe how old someone is or the maturity associated with adult life. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, with “age” appearing as a translation in several passages. Its broad use includes references from Job, Ezekiel, and the Maccabean books, while the exact sense in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “summer,” the warm season of the year. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it names a particular season within the yearly cycle, alongside the other appointed times of the year. The word occurs eight times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages from Genesis, Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its references connect the season with ordinary patterns of time and the natural order, but the word itself simply identifies summer. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This verb means to burn incense, describing the act of offering fragrant material by fire. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used in settings connected with worship and priestly service, including the burning of incense before God. The word occurs 42 times across 40 verses in the Greek Old Testament, so it describes a recurring religious action rather than a rare or specialized event. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is being offered.

This word is the personal name “Iapheth,” also rendered “Iafeth.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, appearing nine times in Genesis and twice in 1 Chronicles. Its first listed occurrence is Genesis 5:32, and its last is 1 Chronicles 1:5. The name itself does not describe a quality or concept; it identifies a particular person in the biblical genealogical record.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Idiēl; Ithil.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:2. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its personal identity and role must be understood from that passage rather than from the name alone.

“Iebosthe” or “Ievosthe” is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the Greek text, all in 2 Samuel. The available references show its use in 2 Samuel 2 and 23, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s role or situation in each passage.

Ieldaph, also rendered Ielthaf, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific person or named figure in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Kings 23:36. Because the supplied information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise identity and role must be determined from that passage. The name itself carries no additional lexical definition beyond identifying the named individual.

Isoui, also identified as Isoi, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It refers to an individual in the Old Testament Greek (LXX) tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 7:30. Its basic function is to distinguish one person from others in the genealogy or list where it appears.

“Israelite” refers to a person belonging to Israel or identifies something associated with an Israelite. It can function as a noun for the person or as a description of identity. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, this word occurs 12 times, appearing mainly in the Old Testament portion and once in 4 Maccabees. Its occurrences include passages in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, and Psalms. The basic meaning remains a plain identifier of Israelite identity rather than a separate title or action.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut down/up”: it describes cutting something down or bringing it down. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, from Genesis through 2 Maccabees. The precise object being cut or brought down depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains forceful downward cutting or destruction.

This Greek LXX noun means “preparation”: the act or result of making something ready or arranging it for a purpose. It can describe readiness, the ordered work involved in setting something up, or the prepared arrangement itself. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central sense remains consistent while its precise application depends on the surrounding passage. It is found especially in descriptions of worship furnishings, offerings, and organized work.

This Greek LXX adverb means “from below” or “up from below.” It describes movement or position in relation to something higher, indicating that a person or object comes from a lower place or is situated underneath. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament, across Exodus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea consistently concerns direction or location from below.

This Greek verb means “mix”: to combine substances or ingredients so they become a blended preparation. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times across Proverbs, Isaiah, and Bel and the Dragon. Its precise force in any individual passage depends on what is being combined, but the central idea remains bringing separate things together.

Koniorton is a proper name used as a specific designation rather than a general description or action. Its meaning is simply “Koniorton,” so the available information does not establish whether it names a person, place, or something else. In the LXX corpus, it occurs eight times across seven verses. Its precise referent must be determined from the verse and surrounding passage.

Leemi is a proper name rendered as “Leemi.” As a name, it identifies rather than describes an action, quality, or object in the ordinary way a common noun does. This Greek LXX word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 20:5. Its specific role in that verse is understood from the passage itself, but the word’s basic lexical function is simply to designate the name Leemi.

This Greek LXX verb means “have leprosy,” describing a person affected by that disease. It functions as an action or condition word rather than a name or title. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within the same verse: Numbers 12:10. The word therefore identifies the presence of leprosy, while the surrounding passage determines what is happening to the person and why the condition matters there.

This adjective means “rest” or “remains”—what is left over after part has been removed, used, or considered. It can describe the remaining people, things, or portion in a group. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 32 times, showing a repeated use for something that continues or is left behind. Its exact English wording depends on the sentence, but the central idea is what remains beyond what has already been addressed.

This word means a “cook-shop,” a place where food is prepared or sold. It is a noun naming the establishment itself rather than the person who cooks or the food being served. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 46:23–24. Without the surrounding verse text, the word’s basic meaning is clear, while the exact details of how the cook-shop functions in those verses must come from the passage’s wider context.

Maserem is a proper name preserved as “Maserem,” not a common word describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 23:14. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or translation meaning. Its precise role in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here. This is a Greek LXX name and should remain distinct from similarly rendered Hebrew or Greek New Testament entities.

Maches is a proper name, rendered “Maches” or “Makhes.” It functions as a name rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Joshua 15:40. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not establish its meaning as an ordinary vocabulary term. Its exact referent is therefore best understood from the surrounding passage rather than by assigning it an additional definition.

This Greek LXX adjective means “drunken,” describing someone affected by excessive alcohol or showing the condition of intoxication. It functions as a describing word rather than naming an action or object. The word occurs five times in the LXX corpus, in Proverbs, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the condition of being drunken.

This adverb means “between” or “meantime,” indicating an interval, position, or situation separating two things or moments. It can describe what occurs in the intervening period or what lies between others. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Wisdom of Solomon. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something situated between or happening in the meantime.

Nabouzardan, also rendered Navuzarthan, is a proper name rather than a general word with an abstract meaning. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs seven times, appearing in passages from 2 Kings and Jeremiah. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense itself is simply this personal name. It is found in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 47, 50, and 52.

This noun means “young man,” referring to a male who is relatively young. It identifies a person by age and sex rather than naming a particular occupation, character quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 29 times, showing regular use for young male persons. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “make,” describing the act of producing, preparing, or arranging something. It is a practical action word rather than a title or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all within the Old Testament books represented in this corpus. Its use includes language about making or preparing, while the exact object and force depend on the sentence where it appears. The central idea remains straightforward: bringing something about, constructing it, or getting it ready for a purpose.

This adjective describes someone or something as deeply deserving pity, sorrow, or lament. It expresses the strongest degree of being pitiable or lamentable, rather than merely ordinary sadness. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:28. Since the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage determines exactly what person or situation receives this description, while the word itself points to an especially distressing or sorrowful condition.

This noun means “company”—the presence or association of people together. It can refer to the company someone keeps or to companionship as a social setting. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented by this LXX corpus, it occurs four times, including passages in Exodus, Proverbs, Wisdom, and 3 Maccabees. Its exact emphasis—whether the people accompanying someone or the association itself—depends on the sentence and surrounding context.

This word is a proper name referring to Ouel, also given as Oil. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, in Ezra 10:34, so it identifies a particular person or name rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. The available wording gives the name itself, but without the verse text it does not establish anything further about the individual or his role in that passage.

gl: entrust sb to; commit sb to
d: entrust sb to; commit sb to

e.t: This verb means to entrust someone to another person or to commit someone into another’s care. It describes deliberately placing a person under someone else’s responsibility, protection, or authority. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX material, both in 2 Maccabees, so its central sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. Its precise force in either passage depends on whom the person is entrusted to and the wider context.

This noun refers to a pelican, a large water bird. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Psalms. Its meaning remains straightforward across these occurrences: it identifies the bird itself rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The English rendering “pelican” agrees with the word’s explicit lexical definition. As with any individual occurrence, the surrounding verse determines why the pelican is mentioned there, but the word’s basic reference is clear.

This noun refers to something formed or devised—a contrivance or a form. It can describe an object shaped by design, emphasizing that it is made rather than naturally occurring. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four different Old Testament verses. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains something fashioned, constructed, or devised.

This noun refers to besieging: placing a city or fortified place under siege. It describes the act or condition of surrounding a place in warfare, usually to pressure those inside to surrender. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Sirach 50:4. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, since the verse text is not included here; its central meaning remains the action of a siege.

This word means “bailiff,” referring to an officer who carries out an authority’s orders or manages an assigned duty. As a noun, it identifies a person rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 3:12. The word’s basic sense is therefore a responsible official serving under someone else’s authority. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to the office or person of a bailiff.

This noun refers to one who stands before others—a front-rank man or person who takes a leading position. Its basic idea is someone placed at the forefront, rather than someone merely present in a group. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs six times, chiefly in Chronicles, with one occurrence in 2 Maccabees. The surrounding passage determines whether the word points to a particular leader or a person holding a prominent place.

Raassōn is a proper name, referring to a person named Raassōn, also rendered Rhaasson. It is not a general term describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs six times, in six Old Testament verses, appearing in 2 Kings and Isaiah. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to identify the person bearing this name.

This Greek LXX noun means “ruin,” referring to a state of collapse, devastation, or destruction. It is a name for the resulting condition rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, all in 1–2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the condition of something brought down or ruined.

This word is a proper name: “Sadōm; Sathom.” It identifies a named person, place, or other specific entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:62. Because the available wording gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding context, its precise referent in that passage cannot be described further here. The alternate form “Sathom” preserves the same named identity in the supplied rendering.

Salō, also written Salo, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once each in Numbers, 1 Chronicles, and Zechariah. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance; those details must come from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word is a proper name rendered as “Seddada” or “Seththatha.” It identifies a named place or person rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general.
